how: Read one section at a time, with a pencil and your Polyatomic Ions, Naming Toolkit and Metals with Multiple Charges sheets.
Each term in **bold** is defined where it first appears.
Tear off the last sheet. Answer its four questions, write the ten definitions, and turn it in.

why.title: Why It Matters
why.text: The box in your kitchen says baking soda. The FDA lists it as sodium bicarbonate, and a chemist may call it sodium hydrogen carbonate. All three names mean one compound, NaHCO_{3}. A systematic name tells you which ions it contains and in what ratio, so you can write its formula.

items.text: Metals lose electrons to become cations; nonmetals gain electrons to become anions.
Main-group ion charges follow the group:
Metals and nonmetals transfer electrons (ionic); nonmetals share electrons (covalent).

vocab.def: a compound made of exactly two elements
a compound made of molecules, in which atoms (usually nonmetals) share electrons in covalent bonds
an ion made of a single atom, such as Na^{+} or Cl^{−}
a group of covalently bonded atoms that carries an overall charge
a negative polyatomic ion in which an element is bonded to oxygen atoms, such as sulfate, SO_{4}^{2−}
the lowest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound
the naming system that shows a metal ion's charge with a Roman numeral in parentheses, as in iron(III)
a compound that produces hydrogen ions (H^{+}) when it dissolves in water
an acid made of hydrogen and one other element, such as HCl
an acid that contains hydrogen, oxygen and at least one other element

body.text: Two nonmetals, more than one compound

Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, and they combine in more than one ratio. One carbon atom with one oxygen atom makes carbon monoxide, CO. One carbon atom with two oxygen atoms makes carbon dioxide, CO_{2} (Figure 6.1). These are different substances. Carbon dioxide is the waste gas you breathe out. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless, poisonous gas. A name like “carbon oxide” would not tell you which one you had.

body.caption: Same two elements, different ratio, different substance. The panel lists atom counts only; it is not a drawing of either molecule.

body.text: Each of these is a **binary compound**, a compound made of exactly two elements. Their atoms share electrons in covalent bonds (Unit 4), so they are covalent compounds. A covalent compound is also called a **molecular compound**, because it is made of molecules: atoms, usually nonmetals, share electrons in covalent bonds. This reading uses the word covalent from here on, as your Naming Toolkit sheet does.

An ionic compound gets its ratio from the charges on its ions, as you will see in Section 6.3. A covalent compound has no ion charges to set the ratio, and the same two nonmetals can often form more than one compound. So a covalent name has to state how many atoms of each element are in the molecule. It does that with prefixes.
Naming with prefixes

The prefixes run from mono- (1) through di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4), penta- (5), hexa- (6), hepta- (7), octa- (8) and nona- (9) to deca- (10). They are on your Naming Toolkit sheet. To name a binary covalent compound from its formula:

items: Name the first element in full. Add a prefix only if there are two or more atoms of it. A name never starts with mono-.
Name the second element with a prefix, mono- included, and change its ending to ‑ide: oxygen becomes oxide, chlorine becomes chloride.
Before “oxide,” drop the last a or o of the prefix: monoxide, tetroxide, pentoxide.

body.text: To go from a name to a formula, turn each prefix back into a subscript. No prefix on the first element means one atom. Never reduce a covalent formula. Dinitrogen tetroxide, N_{2}O_{4}, and nitrogen dioxide, NO_{2}, have the same 1 : 2 ratio, but they are different molecules.

Some compounds skip prefixes by custom. A compound of hydrogen and one other nonmetal is named without them: HCl is hydrogen chloride, not hydrogen monochloride. Water (H_{2}O), ammonia (NH_{3}) and methane (CH_{4}) keep their common names.

body.title: Name N_{2}O.
body.after: Nitrogen gets di- because there are two atoms. Oxygen gets mono- because a second element always takes a prefix, and the o of mono drops before oxide. Check by going back: di- and mono- rebuild N_{2}O.

body.q: Write the formula for sulfur hexafluoride.

solution.note: The missing prefix on sulfur means one atom; a name never starts with mono-.

body.text: Which naming system?

Before you name anything, decide what kind of compound you have (Figure 6.2). Check for an acid first: a formula that starts with H and is written (aq) is an acid in water, and Section 6.4 names it. Next, look for ions. A metal or the ammonium ion, NH_{4}^{+}, means the compound is ionic, and Sections 6.2 and 6.3 apply. Only nonmetals means covalent, so use prefixes.

body.caption: Sort first, then name. An H at the front is not enough to make an acid; the (aq) is the signal.

body.title: One oxygen atom apart
body.text: The CDC describes carbon monoxide as an odorless, colorless gas that can kill you. Furnaces, generators and charcoal grills can all give it off, and you will not see or smell it. Carbon dioxide, with one more oxygen atom, is the waste gas your cells make and your lungs breathe out. The prefix in the name marks the difference.
Ions made of several atoms

Every ion you have used so far, such as Na^{+} or Cl^{−}, has been a **monatomic ion**, an ion made of a single atom. Many ions are not. A **polyatomic ion** is a group of covalently bonded atoms that carries an overall charge.

Ammonium, NH_{4}^{+}, is one nitrogen atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. The group has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so the whole group carries a 1+ charge. The charge belongs to the group, not to any one atom, and the group stays together in a compound. That is why ammonium chloride, NH_{4}Cl, is ionic even though it contains no metal.
Your Polyatomic Ions sheet lists 37 ions. The 15 marked with a star are the ones to memorize, and you can look up the rest. This reading does not reprint the list, so keep the sheet beside you.
Oxyanions and their endings

Look down the negative ions on the sheet and most of them contain oxygen. Each of those is an **oxyanion**, a negative polyatomic ion in which an element is bonded to oxygen atoms, such as sulfate, SO_{4}^{2−}.

Many elements form two oxyanions with the same charge. The one ending in ‑ate has one more oxygen atom than the one ending in ‑ite. Nitrate is NO_{3}^{−} and nitrite is NO_{2}^{−}. Sulfate is SO_{4}^{2−} and sulfite is SO_{3}^{2−}. The ending tells you which of the pair has more oxygen. It does not tell you how many: nitrate has three oxygen atoms and sulfate has four. Learn each ‑ate ion, and work out its ‑ite partner from it.

Chlorine forms four oxyanions, all with a 1− charge (Figure 6.3). Perchlorate, ClO_{4}^{−}, has one more oxygen atom than chlorate, ClO_{3}^{−}. Hypochlorite, ClO^{−}, has one fewer than chlorite, ClO_{2}^{−}. Bromine and iodine follow the same pattern: bromate is BrO_{3}^{−}, iodate is IO_{3}^{−} and periodate is IO_{4}^{−}. Only chlorate is starred; the others are on the sheet for reference.

body.caption: The chlorine ladder. Each step down removes one oxygen atom, and the charge stays 1−.

body.text: Don't stretch the per- and hypo- pattern to every ion. Permanganate, MnO_{4}^{−}, is starred, but there is no manganate on your sheet. Memorize permanganate as a name of its own.
Some ions are a familiar ion with a hydrogen added, and the name adds the word hydrogen. Adding H^{+} makes the charge one less negative: sulfate, SO_{4}^{2−}, becomes hydrogen sulfate, HSO_{4}^{−}.

body.title: Sulfate is SO_{4}^{2−}. Write the formula and charge of sulfite.
body.after: Only the oxygen count changes. Sulfur is still the central element and the charge is still 2−.

body.q: Phosphate, PO_{4}^{3−}, is starred on your sheet. Phosphite is not, but it follows the same pattern. Write the formula and charge of phosphite.

solution.note: A pattern item: phosphite is unstarred (reference only), and its parent, phosphate, is starred. Check it against the sheet.

body.title: Nitrite in cured meat
body.text: Cured meats such as bacon can contain sodium nitrite, NaNO_{2}. According to the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, nitrite helps prevent botulism and keeps cured meat's red color. Sodium nitrate, NaNO_{3}, has one more oxygen atom and is a different compound. On an ingredient label, ‑ite or ‑ate is the difference.
Naming monatomic ions

A monatomic cation keeps the element's name: Na^{+} is the sodium ion, and Ca^{2+} is the calcium ion. A monatomic anion takes the ending ‑ide, so chlorine becomes chloride and oxygen becomes oxide (Figure 6.4).

body.caption: Monatomic anions. Keep the root of the element's name, add ‑ide, and read the charge from the group.

body.text: Don't mix up an element's name with its ion's name. Chlorine is Cl_{2}, a gas made of molecules. Chloride is Cl^{−}, an ion found in compounds such as NaCl. Sodium is a soft metal; the sodium ion is Na^{+}. Seven elements exist as diatomic molecules: H_{2}, N_{2}, O_{2}, F_{2}, Cl_{2}, Br_{2} and I_{2}. They are listed on your Naming Toolkit sheet. That subscript 2 belongs to the element. It never carries over to a monatomic ion inside a compound: sodium chloride is NaCl, not NaCl_{2}.
Charges set the ratio

An ionic compound is held together by the attraction between positive and negative ions (Unit 4). Main-group ions have the charges listed in the Key Refreshers on page 1. In every ionic compound, the positive and negative charges add up to zero.

Ionic compounds are not made of molecules. A crystal of sodium chloride is a huge, repeating arrangement of Na^{+} and Cl^{−} ions, so its formula gives a ratio, not a count. A **formula unit** is the lowest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound. For NaCl, it is one Na^{+} ion for every Cl^{−} ion.
Writing the formula

To write the formula, find the smallest number of each ion that makes the charges cancel. In aluminum oxide, aluminum forms Al^{3+} and oxygen forms O^{2−}. Two Al^{3+} ions give +6 and three O^{2−} ions give −6 (Figure 6.5), so the formula is Al_{2}O_{3}. A shortcut is to cross the charge numbers: aluminum's 3 becomes oxygen's subscript, and oxygen's 2 becomes aluminum's. Then reduce if both subscripts share a factor. Ca^{2+} and O^{2−} give CaO, not Ca_{2}O_{2}. Either way, check that the total is zero.

body.caption: Charge tiles for aluminum oxide. Each tile's length is its charge. Two 3+ tiles match three 2− tiles.

body.text: A polyatomic ion keeps its own formula. When a compound needs more than one of it, put the ion in parentheses and write the count outside: calcium nitrate is Ca(NO_{3})_{2}, one Ca^{2+} for every two NO_{3}^{−}. Never change the subscripts inside the ion. NO_{3} is nitrate, and any other subscript makes a different ion.

To name an ionic compound, name the cation first and the anion second, each as above. A polyatomic ion keeps its name. Ionic names don't use prefixes to count ions. CaCl_{2} is calcium chloride, because the charges already fix the ratio.
Metals with more than one charge

Sodium forms only one ion, Na^{+}, so “sodium chloride” can only mean NaCl. Many transition metals form more than one ion. Iron forms Fe^{2+} and Fe^{3+}, so “iron chloride” could mean FeCl_{2} or FeCl_{3}. The **Stock system** is the naming system that shows a metal ion's charge with a Roman numeral in parentheses, as in iron(III). FeCl_{2} is iron(II) chloride, and FeCl_{3} is iron(III) chloride. The numeral is the charge on one metal ion. It is not the number of metal atoms.

Your Metals with Multiple Charges sheet lists the metals that need a numeral. Metals such as silver (Ag^{+}), zinc (Zn^{2+}) and cadmium (Cd^{2+}) have one common charge, so their names take no numeral.

Starting from a formula, work back from the anion, because you know its charge (Figure 6.6). The total negative charge tells you the total positive charge. Divide that total by the number of metal ions to get the charge on each one.

body.title: Name Fe_{2}O_{3}.
body.after: Iron forms two ions, so the name needs the numeral. The III is the charge on each iron ion, not the two iron atoms in the formula.

body.caption: Working back from the anion. The oxide ions fix the total, and the two iron ions split it.

body.q: Write the formula for lead(II) nitrate. Check that the charges add up to zero.

solution.note: Parentheses because there are two nitrate ions. The II is lead's charge, not a subscript.

body.text: Older names

You may see older names like ferrous (Fe^{2+}) and ferric (Fe^{3+}), or cuprous (Cu^{+}) and cupric (Cu^{2+}), on labels and in older books. ‑ous is the lower charge and ‑ic the higher. The Roman-numeral name is the modern standard because it states the charge. The ending tells you lower or higher, not the number: ferrous is 2+ but cuprous is 1+. These metal endings have nothing to do with the acid endings in Section 6.4.

body.title: Two iron oxides
body.text: Iron(II) oxide, FeO, is a black solid. Iron(III) oxide, Fe_{2}O_{3}, is red-brown; it is the mineral hematite, and red ochre is colored by it. The two oxides have the same elements, a different charge on iron, a different ratio and a different color. The Roman numeral tells you which one you have.
What makes an acid

An **acid** is a compound that produces hydrogen ions (H^{+}) when it dissolves in water. Unit 14 widens this definition. Acid names depend on that water. Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is a gas. Dissolved in water and written HCl(aq), it is hydrochloric acid. The (aq) means dissolved in water, and it is your signal to use an acid name.

Each acid in this section is hydrogen ions paired with an anion. The name comes from the anion's ending, and the formula comes from the anion's charge: one H^{+} for each negative charge (Figure 6.7).

body.caption: The anion's ending decides the acid's name. Only an ‑ide anion takes hydro-.

body.text: Binary acids and oxyacids

A **binary acid** is an acid made of hydrogen and one other element, such as HCl. Its anion ends in ‑ide, so its name takes hydro- at the front and ‑ic acid at the end. Chloride gives hydrochloric acid, and bromide gives hydrobromic acid, HBr(aq).

An **oxyacid** is an acid that contains hydrogen, oxygen and at least one other element. Its anion is an oxyanion, and its name has no hydro-. An ‑ate ion gives an ‑ic acid, and an ‑ite ion gives an ‑ous acid. Nitrate gives nitric acid, HNO_{3}, and nitrite gives nitrous acid, HNO_{2}. A per- or hypo- prefix stays, so perchlorate gives perchloric acid and hypochlorite gives hypochlorous acid.

Sulfur and phosphorus keep more of the element's name. Sulfate gives sulfuric acid, H_{2}SO_{4}, sulfite gives sulfurous acid, H_{2}SO_{3}, and phosphate gives phosphoric acid, H_{3}PO_{4}. Here ‑ous and ‑ic come from the anion's ‑ite or ‑ate ending, not from a metal's charge as in the older names of Section 6.3.

body.title: Name HNO_{3}(aq).
body.after: The anion contains oxygen, so this is an oxyacid and hydro- is not used. One H balances nitrate's 1− charge, which matches the formula.

body.q: Write the formula for carbonic acid. Name the anion it comes from first.

body.title: Carbonated drinks
body.text: A soda is bottled with carbon dioxide dissolved in it. Some of that CO_{2} reacts with water to form carbonic acid:
body.after: The double arrow means the reaction runs in both directions. The name carbonic acid tells you the anion it is built on: carbonate, CO_{3}^{2−}.

questions.q: Why do the names of covalent compounds need prefixes?
questions.answer: The same two nonmetals can form more than one compound (CO and CO_{2}), and a covalent compound has no ion charges to set the ratio, so the name has to state how many atoms of each element there are.
questions.accept: Full credit needs both reasons: more than one possible compound, and no charges to fix the ratio.

questions.q: What do the endings ‑ate and ‑ite tell you about nitrate and nitrite?
questions.answer: The ‑ate ion has one more oxygen atom than the ‑ite ion, with the same charge: nitrate is NO_{3}^{−} and nitrite is NO_{2}^{−}.
questions.accept: The ending gives more or fewer oxygen atoms, not the number. A student who writes only the formulas without stating the one-oxygen difference has not answered the question.

questions.q: Why does iron(III) chloride need a Roman numeral when sodium chloride does not?
questions.answer: Iron forms two ions, Fe^{2+} and Fe^{3+}, so the numeral shows which one is present. Sodium forms only Na^{+}, so its name needs no numeral.

questions.q: How does an acid's name show which anion it came from?
questions.answer: The ending follows the anion's ending: an ‑ate ion gives an ‑ic acid, an ‑ite ion gives an ‑ous acid, and an ‑ide ion gives a hydro- … ‑ic acid.
questions.accept: An example such as nitrate → nitric acid, nitrite → nitrous acid shows the rule.

tearOff.vocabNote: Write each definition in your own words, using the reading. Each term is in bold where it is first defined.

teacherNotes: Not test-allowed. The reading teaches the ionic, covalent and acid naming procedures that the reference packet deliberately leaves out (Naming Toolkit, sheet 7: no naming procedure, so the test packet does not answer naming items). Treat it as not test-allowed material.

Key Refreshers (cover, SHULL-CHG-0117) are three short reminders, one per column of the Before You Begin box, from 3.7 Ion Formation and 4.2/4.3 Ionic and Covalent Bonding, the unit's builds-on in the U6 roadmap. They reteach nothing and are not on the tear-off. Cation and anion appear there unbolded; the ten bold terms are unchanged. The main-group charges are stated only in the refresher, as a small group/charge table that includes Group 13, aluminum (Al^{3+}), and Section 6.3 points back to it.

Element vs ion names (6.3). Watch for NaCl_{2} and “chlorine” used for Cl^{−}. The diatomic list is the Naming Toolkit's seven (H, N, O, F, Cl, Br, I). The ion table (Figure 6.4) gives the eight monatomic anions students name most; each charge comes from its group.

Oxide spelling (Matt's D5). The reading drops the vowel before “oxide” (monoxide, tetroxide, pentoxide), as most US textbooks and the deck do. IUPAC (2005) keeps it (tetraoxide, pentaoxide) and elides only “monoxide.” Accept either spelling.

Classical names (D4). The student note gives Fe and Cu only. Others on the Metals with Multiple Charges sheet: stannous Sn^{2+} / stannic Sn^{4+}; plumbous Pb^{2+} / plumbic Pb^{4+}; cobaltous Co^{2+} / cobaltic Co^{3+} (cobaltic chloride, CoCl_{3}, is a disputed compound). Mercury is left out on purpose: mercurous is Hg_{2}^{2+}, and printing mercuric alone invites the wrong guess Hg^{+}. IUPAC no longer recommends ‑ous/‑ic metal names; they are still used on labels and in older books.

Carbonated drinks (Connection 6.4). Most dissolved CO_{2} stays as CO_{2}; only a small fraction becomes H_{2}CO_{3} (hydration constant about 1.7 × 10^{−3} at 25 °C). The reading says “some” for that reason.

On Your Own 6.2 uses phosphite, which is on sheet 6 but unstarred; it is a pattern item built on starred phosphate. Carbonate → hydrogen carbonate was not used because sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO_{3}, is named in Why It Matters. Don't extend phosphite to an acid item: phosphorous acid, H_{3}PO_{3}, has one H bonded to P and gives up only two H^{+}, and free PO_{3}^{3−} is not a real species in water.

The per-/‑ate/‑ite/hypo- ladder is stated for the halogens only. Permanganate is a name to memorize, not a ladder member (manganate, MnO_{4}^{2−}, differs in charge, not oxygen count). Dichromate, thiosulfate and thiocyanate are not ladder members either. Hydroxide is not usually counted as an oxyanion.

HCN is kept out of student items. If it comes up: cyanide ends in ‑ide, so HCN(aq) is hydrocyanic acid, but it has three elements and is not a binary acid. That is why 6.4 teaches the rule by the anion's ending.

The common name of N_{2}O (Example 6.1) is nitrous oxide. It is kept off the student page so it is not confused with nitrous acid. Sheet 6 calls HS^{−} “hydrogen sulfide,” the usual name for H_{2}S gas; the reading avoids both.

Acid definition: in water, H^{+} attaches to a water molecule as H_{3}O^{+} (hydronium, starred on sheet 6). Unit 14 widens the definition. The Roman numeral in a Stock name is the oxidation number, which equals the charge for a monatomic ion.
IUPAC spellings differ from the school ones used here: oxoacid, oxoanion, monoatomic, hydrogencarbonate (one word). The reading keeps the spellings on the student's sheets.

Figure 6.1 is a counts-only panel with no structure: two labelled boxes giving each formula, name and atom tally (Matt's ruling, 2026-11-25, “Counts-only panel”). The shared molecule builder drew CO with a misleading formal charge (O^{+} with no C^{−} label) or as a double bond, so no molecule is drawn in this reading.
